category.text: $course$/Game Theory/Chapter 06 - Extensive-Form Games, Backward Induction and Subgame Perfection (Quiz)

questiontext.text: In the entry game (entrant chooses In or Out; if In, the incumbent chooses Fight giving \((-2, -2)\) or Accommodate giving \((2, 5)\); Out gives \((0, 10)\)), what does backward induction predict?

generalfeedback.text: Start at the incumbent's node: \(5 \gt -2\), so Accommodate. Folding back, the entrant compares 2 from entering with 0 from staying out and enters. The prediction is (In, Accommodate) with payoffs (2, 5).

feedback.text: That is a Nash equilibrium but relies on a non-credible threat.

answer.text: The game has no solution by backward induction

feedback.text: It is finite with perfect information, so Zermelo applies.

questiontext.text: Every subgame perfect Nash equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium, but not every Nash equilibrium is subgame perfect.

generalfeedback.text: True. SPNE requires Nash behaviour in the whole game and in every subgame, so it is a strictly stronger requirement. The entry game's (Out, Fight) is Nash but not subgame perfect.

questiontext.text: What makes the incumbent's threat to fight non-credible?

generalfeedback.text: Credibility is about incentives at the moment of action, not about what was announced. If entry occurs, fighting yields \(-2\) and accommodating yields \(5\), so the incumbent would not carry out the threat. This is exactly what subgame perfection checks.

answer.text: If entry actually happened, fighting would give the incumbent a strictly lower payoff than accommodating
The incumbent has no way to communicate the threat

feedback.text: Communication is not the issue; incentives are.

answer.text: Fighting is a strictly dominated strategy in the strategic form

feedback.text: It is not strictly dominated there, which is why the Nash concept misses the problem.

answer.text: The entrant cannot observe the incumbent's move

feedback.text: The entrant moves first and needs no observation.

questiontext.text: Player 1 moves first with 2 possible actions. Player 2 then moves, observing player 1's choice, and has 3 actions available at each of player 1's two nodes. How many distinct strategies does player 2 have?

generalfeedback.text: A strategy for player 2 assigns an action to each of the two information sets, so there are 3 x 3 = 9 strategies. This blow-up is why the strategic form of even a small tree can be large.

questiontext.text: Inverse demand \(P = 100 - Q\), unit cost \(c = 10\), firm 1 moves first. What quantity does the leader produce?

generalfeedback.text: The leader anticipates \(q_2 = (a - c - q_1)/2\) and maximises, giving \(q_1^{*} = \dfrac{a - c}{2} = 45\). The follower then produces \(\dfrac{a - c}{4} = 22.5\). Both Cournot firms would have produced 30 each.

questiontext.text: Same setting (\(P = 100 - Q\), \(c = 10\), sequential choice). What quantity does the follower produce?

generalfeedback.text: \(q_2^{*} = \dfrac{a - c}{4} = 22.5\). The follower is squeezed below its Cournot output of 30 because the leader's commitment to 45 leaves less residual demand.

questiontext.text: Deliberately restricting your own future options can raise your payoff.

generalfeedback.text: True, and this is one of the most useful ideas in the subject. Removing an option changes what others expect you to do at future nodes. Burning bridges, signing penalty clauses, and delegating to a hard-line negotiator all work by making a threat credible that would otherwise not be.

questiontext.text: Backward induction in the centipede game predicts the first player takes immediately, yet experimental subjects usually pass for several rounds. The best reading of this gap is:

generalfeedback.text: Backward induction needs common knowledge of rationality to survive at nodes that would only be reached if someone had already deviated from it. Once a player passes, the assumption that generated the prediction is in doubt. Experimental evidence also shows limited depth of reasoning and genuine other-regarding preferences.

answer.text: Backward induction relies on common knowledge of rationality holding even at nodes that would only be reached after a deviation from it
The game has no subgame perfect equilibrium

feedback.text: It has one, computed by backward induction.

answer.text: Subjects cannot compute the equilibrium because it is PPAD-complete

feedback.text: The tree is small and the computation is easy.

answer.text: Backward induction is mathematically invalid in finite trees

feedback.text: It is valid; the question is whether its assumptions describe people.
